claims.text: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be produced in bulk form by additive manufacturing followed by sintering.
The printed and sintered bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be nearly fully densified and contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Spark plasma sintering is a suitable route for producing the stated nearly fully densified, approximately 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr state.
The approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen has associated realistic lattice-defect distributions relevant to conductivity.
A first-principles/machine-learning or CALPHAD-based model can incorporate oxygen-impurity scattering and realistic defects into electronic and phononic conduction calculations.
Conductivity measurements exist or can be compared with predictions for approximately 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Conductivity measurements exist or can be compared with predictions for approximately 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Quantum and impurity-scattering effects dominate conductivity behavior in the 0–200 K regime.
Enhanced phonon scattering and defect-related mechanisms become significant over 300–1200 K.
Oxygen and other defects create states that locally change electron-scattering rates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen and other defects change lattice dynamics and thereby alter effective conductivity relative to a defect-free crystal.
Explicit treatment of oxygen impurities and defect distributions accounts for temperature-dependent electron–phonon and impurity scattering.
Accounting for these scattering mechanisms will improve the accuracy of the predicted conductivity-versus-temperature curve relative to ideal-crystal analytical models.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr generally assume a perfect, defect-free crystal.
Failure to include impurity and defect scattering causes significant discrepancies between existing analytical predictions and measurements on oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
For the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen, predicted conductivity over 300–1200 K will be within 10–15% of experiment.
Over 0–200 K, the model will capture increased impurity scattering that is absent from perfect-crystal models.
The proposed accuracy advantage applies to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content near 1 wt.% over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model accuracy may diminish above 1200 K because phase changes or oxidation can become dominant.
Model accuracy depends on characterization of defect types and distributions and may require separate calibration at very low and high temperatures.

contradictions.description: The prediction uses an absolute error target of 10–15% relative to experiment, whereas the falsification rule uses a 10–15% reduction in error relative to an ideal-crystal model. These are different benchmarks, so the stated success and falsification criteria are not directly complementary.
